West Hartford at a glance

Five miles west of downtown Hartford, West Hartford spreads over 22.3 square miles of Hartford County, and 64,083 people lived there in 2020. Its neighbors are Bloomfield, Newington, New Britain, Farmington and Avon, the Metacomet Ridge runs along its west side, and the high point is 778 feet on Talcott (Avon) Mountain, against 120 feet at Town Hall.

Locals know the town by its centers. West Hartford Center is the old commercial hub around Farmington Avenue and South and North Main Street. Elmwood, in the southeast, grew around the railroad and factories. Interstate 84 was built through town by 1969, and that cut Elmwood off from the rest. Bishops Corner opened as a shopping district in 1971, and Westfarms Mall sits on the southwest edge beside the interstate.

Two houses a mile apart can belong to very different pockets, so check the bill for your own parcel instead of assuming a neighbor's applies to you.

Why the housing stock is mixed

Settlers came around 1679, and on May 3, 1854 the former Hartford parish became a town of its own. The bulk of the houses arrived afterward, in three waves.

  • Streetcar suburbs: trolley lines reached the countryside in 1889, and subdivisions such as Buena Vista (1895) and Elmhurst (1901) followed.
  • The 1920s: West Hill was planned with design restrictions and is a National Historic District, and the population rose from 4,808 in 1910 to 24,941 in 1930.
  • The postwar boom: the town grew from 33,776 residents in 1940 to 62,382 in 1960 and built one new elementary school every year in the 1950s.

West Hartford adopted zoning in 1924, the first Connecticut municipality to do so. Old zoning rules and old additions can complicate a sale, so keep past permits handy.

Who bills and collects the tax

The Tax Office at Town Hall bills and collects West Hartford property tax. Find it at 50 South Main Street, Room 109, or call 860-561-7474, option 4, Monday to Friday from 8:30 AM to 4:30 PM.

A Delinquent Tax Collector sits on the staff for unpaid bills. The town also uses TaxServ Capital Services, but only for delinquent motor vehicle and business personal property tax, so the town office itself handles a house payoff. The Tax Office page carries current figures, and its FAQ page covers penalty and relief questions.

Rates for the 2025 Grand List are 46.77 for real estate and business personal property and 32.46 for motor vehicles. Online payments carry fees of $0.90 for e-check, or 2.99% with a $3.95 minimum for cards, PayPal or Venmo.

The next installment on the calendar is the one due January 1, 2027. Call the Tax Office for your exact balance and for the last day to pay each bill without penalty.

How do the two installments matter when you sell?

Whatever installment is open on closing day becomes part of the sale. The summer bill and the winter bill split the year, so a spring or fall closing typically leaves one of them still to come.

Request a written balance before you sign. Tell the office your likely closing date, then ask which amounts are paid, which are open and whether the Delinquent Tax Collector holds anything. A Look Up My Tax Info tool and a refund request form on the town's page help when a bill was paid twice or a bank was supposed to pay it.

If a mortgage servicer handles your escrow, confirm with both the servicer and the office that the same bill is not paid twice. With a cash sale and no mortgage, the title company usually pays open tax from your proceeds, and the amount should match what the office quotes.

Assessment questions

Questions about how a value was set belong with the town's Assessment Office, since the Tax Office only bills and collects. If your bill changed sharply, read the Tax Office page titled How Revaluation Impacts Taxes. If an appeal is pending, ask whether it alters the due date on your bill.

When you call, have your parcel address and the most recent bill nearby, and write down what the person tells you.

What the state requires when a house is sold

A seller in Connecticut owes the state a conveyance tax return, Form OP-236, at the time the deed goes on record. A price of $2,000 or more triggers the tax, subject to exemptions.

  • Whoever acts for the grantor, whether the grantor, an attorney or an authorized agent, submits the return and pays at recording.
  • On the state form, West Hartford carries town code 155.
  • In participating towns the filing can go through myCTREC, and the money is drawn only once the town clerk has recorded the deed.
  • A town without electronic filing wants both pages of the form at the clerk's counter, plus a check payable to the Commissioner of Revenue Services.

Two exemptions are the ones that stressed sellers ask about: selling a principal residence for too little to cover the mortgages plus the real estate tax and other liens ranking ahead of them, and conveying a principal residence in lieu of foreclosure. A pyrrhotite-damaged foundation under a principal residence can qualify as well, though only with an engineer's written evaluation. Your closing attorney will choose the code. The state conveyance tax page has the full list.

Behind on tax and selling

An overdue bill is not a barrier to selling. Get a written payoff figure from the Tax Office ahead of closing, and the title company can pay the open tax out of your proceeds, with nothing due from you in advance.

Owners who contact us tend to have an inherited house, a difficult tenant, a long list of repairs or a bill that slipped behind. A cash buyer accepts the house as it sits, aging roof and heating system included, so those fixes can wait. Choose whichever route you like, and gather every payoff in one spot first so you can see what the sale will net.

After the closing, hold on to the settlement statement and the Tax Office's payoff letter. They show the bill was cleared, which helps if a question comes up later about who paid what.

Frequently asked questions

Who do I call about West Hartford property tax?

Call the West Hartford Tax Office at 860-561-7474, option 4. The office is in Town Hall at 50 South Main Street, Room 109, and is open Monday to Friday from 8:30 AM to 4:30 PM.

What is the West Hartford mill rate?

The Tax Office lists 46.77 for real estate and business personal property and 32.46 for motor vehicles on the 2025 Grand List.

When is the next West Hartford installment due?

Bills are due July 1 and January 1. The next one is January 1, 2027, and payment is due no later than the first business day in February.

Do I have to file anything with the state when I sell?

Yes. The seller files Form OP-236 with the town clerk when the deed is recorded, and the state conveyance tax is due when the price is $2,000 or more, unless an exemption applies. West Hartford's town code is 155.

Can I sell a West Hartford house that owes back tax?

Yes. Ask the Tax Office for a written payoff figure before closing. The title company can pay open tax from the proceeds, so you do not need cash up front.

Stamford at a glance

Stamford is the largest city in Connecticut by area and the second most populous after Bridgeport, with 135,470 residents in 2020. It lies in Fairfield County on Long Island Sound, about 34 miles from New York City and 79 miles from Hartford. Of its 52.03 square miles, 37.62 are land and 14.41 are water, including harbor, shoreline and islands such as Cove Island and Grass Island.

Interstate 95 and the Merritt Parkway cross the city. Stamford's Metro-North station on the New Haven Line is the second busiest on the system after Grand Central Terminal, and Amtrak's Acela and Northeast Regional trains stop there too. Glenbrook and Springdale have their own commuter stops on the New Canaan branch.

Neighborhoods and why bills differ

Roughly 45 neighborhoods and villages make up the city, along with two historic districts. These names are used most often.

  • Downtown, the South End and Harbor Point, the waterfront redevelopment.
  • Shippan, Cove and Waterside along the Sound.
  • Glenbrook and Springdale.
  • Turn of River, Newfield, Belltown, Ridgeway and Westover.
  • North Stamford, the largest and least dense section, above the Merritt Parkway.

With so much variety, two houses of the same size can carry quite different tax bills. Look up the bill for your own parcel rather than leaning on a citywide average. Greenwich and Darien are neighbors, so owners sometimes compare bills across the line, but a comparison only means something if you check each town's current mill rate and assessment.

Who values your house and who bills it?

Stamford's Assessor's Office values real estate parcel by parcel. The Office of the Tax Collector bills and collects the tax. Phone both offices for the current mill rate, the due dates for the installments and the deadline to appeal an assessment. A decision that depends on a date should rest on what those offices tell you, not on an old bill or a neighbor's memory.

Assessment and appeals fall under Connecticut General Statutes chapter 203. Suppose the assessed value looks too high. Ask the Assessor's Office how a review works, and collect evidence: recent sales of comparable houses, photos of defects and any appraisal you already hold. An appeal that comes with documents is easier to evaluate.

Storm damage and flood zones

Stamford's coastal setting brings hot summers, cold and variable winters and a history of hurricanes and tropical storms on the Connecticut shore, with landfalls in 1903, 1938, 1944, 1954, 1960, 1985 (Gloria) and 2012 (Sandy). For waterfront and low-lying houses, flood zone status, flood insurance and storm repair come up in almost every sale conversation.

If a storm or fire has changed your house, ask the Assessor's Office whether and how that could affect the assessment, and ask before the bill arrives.

State ruleHow it applies in Stamford
Collection lawConnecticut General Statutes chapter 204 covers local levy and collection, including installments, delinquent interest and tax sales

For the current mill rate and appeal dates, call the Assessor and the Tax Collector before you make a decision that depends on them.

How does the conveyance tax work on a Stamford sale?

Recording a deed in Stamford obliges the seller to submit the Connecticut Real Estate Conveyance Tax Return. Form OP-236 comes from the grantor, the grantor's attorney or an authorized agent, and it is due at the moment of recording.

Tax starts at a price of $2,000. If a sale needs several deeds, the combined price is what gets taxed. Town clerks in participating towns take the return online through myCTREC.

Three exemptions deserve a look. Handing a principal residence to the lender in lieu of foreclosure is exempt. So is selling a principal residence for less than the mortgages plus the real estate taxes and municipal liens ahead of them. The third reaches certain sellers who were approved for state or local tax relief for the elderly or disabled, although the municipal portion still has to be paid. Which code goes on the return is a decision for your closing attorney.

Property tax when you sell

Whatever the property owes comes out of your proceeds at the closing table, and the title or closing attorney sets up the payoff. An installment that has not come due or been billed is usually split between you and the buyer for the days each of you owns the house.

Behind on tax? Then a mortgage in arrears, a contractor's lien or an unsettled estate may be in the picture too. Write each payoff on a single sheet, the Tax Collector's written figure beside the lender's, and the realistic net from the sale becomes visible. A shortfall is far easier to handle before a contract is signed than after.

When taxes go unpaid

The state's collection chapter spells out what follows an unpaid bill, with sections on interest on delinquent installments, demand and levy, and the method of selling real estate for taxes. A tax becomes uncollectible after fifteen years. Another section lets a town add municipal expenses to a tax bill when a property violates health, safety or housing codes, so ask whether a code enforcement charge is attached to your address.

Even a balance swollen by interest can be cleared at closing. Ask the Tax Collector for a written payoff dated near the closing day so the figure is current, and keep that letter with your records.

Taxes and a cash sale

A buyer who pays cash does not change what the city is owed. The same payoff, proration and conveyance return apply, and the attorney handles them the same way. The difference is timing: with no lender review in the middle, the closing can land soon after title work is finished, so get your written payoff figures early.

It also means a balance you were hoping to sort out later has to be dealt with by closing day. If you are unsure what you owe, start with a call to the Tax Collector, and bring any notices you have received to your attorney.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

A step-by-step plan for a sale

  1. Phone both city offices and get your assessment, any open balance and the date of the next installment.
  2. If a mortgage exists, request a payoff statement from the lender.
  3. Give your attorney the deed, the tax bills and any lien notices.
  4. Let the attorney choose any exemption code for the conveyance return.
  5. At closing, check that each payoff on the settlement statement matches the written figures.

File the tax receipts and the final settlement statement together, because you may need them at tax time.

Frequently asked questions

Who bills property tax in Stamford, Connecticut?

The city's Assessor's Office values property and the Office of the Tax Collector bills and collects the tax. Confirm current due dates and the mill rate directly with those offices.

Can I sell a Stamford house with unpaid property tax?

Yes. The balance, including interest, is paid from the sale proceeds at closing, and the closing attorney requests a written payoff from the Tax Collector.

What is the Stamford town code on the conveyance tax form?

The state lists 135 as the Stamford code on Form OP-236.

Does Connecticut tax the transfer of a house?

Yes. A real estate conveyance tax is due when the deed is recorded and the price is $2,000 or more, unless an exemption applies. The seller's side files the return.

Is a house sold for less than the debt exempt from the state conveyance tax?

A principal residence is exempt when the price is not enough to pay the mortgages plus the real estate taxes and municipal liens that have priority. The seller claims the exemption on the return.

New Haven housing in brief

New Haven wraps around a harbor where Long Island Sound meets the Connecticut shore. The city spans about 20.1 square miles, with roughly 1.4 of them water, and had 134,023 residents in 2020. Low ground along the harbor and three rivers (the West, the Mill and the Quinnipiac) sits beside East Rock and West Rock, and neighborhoods such as Westville, East Rock, Fair Haven, the Hill, Wooster Square and the East Shore each work as their own market.

Renters occupy about 72 percent of homes, so many sellers here are landlords. Yale is both the biggest employer and the biggest taxpayer. County government in Connecticut ended in 1960, which means no separate county bill arrives. Everything the city pays for, schools included, is billed once.

Due dates and how to pay

The tax year follows the city's fiscal year, July 1 through June 30. Half is due on July 1 and half on January 1. One bill goes out, typically in June, and tax is payable in advance. The city's pay taxes page has the payment methods, summarized here.

Put the tax account number on every mailed check. An online payment made before 8 PM Monday to Thursday posts the following business day; later payments may take 48 hours or longer. Close to a deadline, use cash, a money order or a bank check so no hold delays credit. For the present interest charge on late payments, call the Tax Collector.

Who pays the bill after a sale?

For people buying a house, the city's message is that the next bill due after closing, July 1 or January 1, belongs to the buyer. How the period already under way is shared between the two sides is a question for the closing attorney.

Some state rules can reach a sale. Chapter 204 of the General Statutes has one section about receipts for partial payments when property changes hands and another about municipal costs for health, safety or housing code violations being added to the bill. It also lets a municipality abate the part of a tax above 8 percent of an owner's income. The owner then signs a reimbursement agreement, recorded as a lien, that must be repaid in full once the property is sold or the last owner dies.

Selling a rental property

Because so many New Haven homes are rented, a lot of sales involve tenants. Read each lease first and note its end date, then decide whether you will offer the house occupied or empty. A cash buyer who takes the property as-is may accept it with tenants still living there, which spares you from setting a move-out schedule. If you do need access for showings, give tenants clear written notice and work around their schedule.

Landlords should also pull together rent, utility and repair records, because a buyer's attorney will want them and a tidy file speeds things up. If a tenant is behind or a unit has code problems, say so to your attorney early. Code charges can be added to the tax bill, and the proceeds then absorb them.

Asking the Tax Collector the right questions

Have the tax account number in front of you before you call, since the office finds your record by it. Request the balance for each installment on its own: the July 1 installment covers July through December and the January 1 installment covers January through June. Ask whether anything besides tax has been added. Get the reply in writing so you can pass it to your attorney. Paying at the counter? Cards are refused there and a personal check sits on a five business day hold, so a bank check or money order works better when time is short. Allow for the post-payment delay too, since a payment that has not posted can still show as owed on a payoff statement.

Before you list or take a cash offer

Have your attorney or title company report on every installment, any code-enforcement charge and any recorded abatement lien before you take an offer. Ground close to the rivers and shoreline can mean damp basements, so look over the roof, gutters and heating system, and find out from your lender or title company whether a flood zone map covers the lot. Buyers who work at the universities or the hospital judge condition closely, and pockets like East Rock and Westville draw different offers than areas farther out.

Timing a New Haven closing around the installments

Because the July 1 payment covers the first half of the fiscal year and the January 1 payment covers the second, the date you close decides how much tax is still open and which side carries it. A closing in June, just before a new bill is mailed, leaves the buyer holding a bill that is about to arrive. A closing in late autumn comes after the July 1 installment has already fallen due, so that half should be settled or shown as paid. Neither timing is better or worse, but each should be spelled out in the contract so nobody is surprised by a bill after the keys change hands.

Remember too that taxes here are payable in advance, which can leave a seller who prepaid an installment expecting a credit. Raise that early with your closing attorney, who sets how the current period is divided between the two parties.

Selling with taxes owed

Unpaid tax does not stop a New Haven sale, since closing takes the balance out of your proceeds. The working list is brief:

  • Get the exact balance from the Tax Collector, by installment, using your account number.
  • Check with the Assessor's Office about any pending appeal or correction, since either one could change the figure.
  • Let your closing attorney confirm liens and code charges, and ask for the results before you set a date.
  • Set a cash offer beside the cost of repairs and of carrying the house through another installment.

An as-is cash buyer spares you repairs and showings. Read any offer closely, and have a lawyer look at it.

Bring the latest bill, a photo ID and the deed to your first meeting with the closing attorney, along with the papers showing who may sign if the house is part of an estate.

Frequently asked questions

When is New Haven property tax due?

Half is due July 1 and half January 1, on a July 1 to June 30 fiscal year. The city mails one bill, usually in June.

Where do I pay New Haven property tax in person?

Go to the Tax Collector at 165 Church St, 1st floor, Monday to Friday 9 AM to 5 PM. Cash, checks, money orders and bank checks work there; debit and credit cards do not.

Who pays the tax at a New Haven closing?

The buyer owns the next bill that falls due after closing, and your closing attorney decides how the current period is split.

Is there a county property tax in New Haven?

No. Connecticut ended county government in 1960, so one city bill covers local services and schools.

Can I sell my New Haven house if I owe taxes?

Yes. Your proceeds cover the unpaid tax through the title company, so request a payoff figure before closing.

Greenwich in brief

Two things shape value more than most: the commute (four Metro-North stations, with express trains to Grand Central in about 50 minutes and locals in about 60) and water. Old Greenwich, Riverside and Byram hug the shore, which makes flood zone status a routine question, and the Back Country above the Merritt Parkway collects more snow than the coast does.

Due dates and payment fees

Greenwich rolls real estate, personal property and motor vehicle tax into a single bill. It goes out in June with payment due July 1, and in the latest cycle on the Tax Collector's page the bill went delinquent after August 3. Mailing and delinquency dates shift between years, so trust the bill in your hand.

Visit the Tax Collector in Town Hall, 101 Field Point Road, Room 145, weekdays 8:30 am to 3:30 pm, or phone 203-622-7891.

Interest on a late real estate bill runs to a stated date, and a lien goes on any property that still has a balance in May. Behind on the bill? Get a payoff number from the office first, then pick your closing date.

Where to file a Greenwich assessment appeal

Appeals go to an elected body, the Board of Assessment Appeals. The Assessor's Office turns away appeal forms, which catches out owners who assume the assessor is the right door. The Board's page has the form and the email address, boardofassessmentappeals@greenwichct.org.

Under Connecticut General Statutes section 12-111, real estate and personal property filings close in February at 5:00 pm. The 2025 Grand List cutoff was February 20, with in-person hearings at Town Hall that March. The 2026 Grand List will have its own posted date, so confirm it with the Board before relying on any day.

  • An appeal disputes the assessment alone. The mill rate comes from the Board of Estimate and Taxation each May.
  • The result can be a higher value, a lower one or no change, and notices go out roughly two weeks after the final hearing.

Its five members are elected every two years, in odd-numbered years.

The state conveyance tax return

Recording a deed in Greenwich triggers a state filing, Form OP-236, signed by the seller or the seller's attorney. The town code to enter is 057. Consideration of $2,000 or more is taxed unless the transfer is exempt.

The exempt list on the Department of Revenue Services tax information page names transfers between spouses, a deed in lieu of foreclosure on a principal residence, and a principal residence sold for less than the mortgages and tax liens against it. Ask your closing agent or the Town Clerk's office which line fits your deal.

Selling a Greenwich house with taxes owed

Owing tax does not rule out selling. The balance is subtracted from what you receive at closing, so your real task is learning the number early. Here is a workable order.

  1. Request a payoff on the real estate account from the Tax Collector, interest included.
  2. Ask if a lien has been recorded. Balances get liened in May, and the release must be arranged as part of closing.
  3. Hand the payoff to your closing attorney, who builds it into the settlement statement.
  4. Set the closing date after the lien question is answered, not before.

A lien is not the end of the road. Once the payoff is paid at closing, the lien is released and the buyer receives clear title. Allow a little extra time on the calendar for the release paperwork, particularly if closing falls close to a month-end or a holiday.

Bring the bill, a photo ID and, for an estate, the papers showing who may sign. Because a missed May date can turn a small balance into a lien, even owners who are only slightly behind should call early.

Before you call any office, put three things on the table: the latest tax bill, the assessment notice and the property record. Check the bill for the account number, since the Tax Collector will ask for it. Check the record for square footage, bathroom count and any addition, because an error there carries straight into the assessment and gives you something concrete to bring to the Board. Write down every call: who you spoke with, the date and the figure quoted. A written payoff is what your closing attorney actually needs, and a verbal number from last month will not do.

What Greenwich sellers usually face

Coastal sections, village centers and the Back Country make Greenwich a town where the street decides the story. Houses needing repairs sit longer on the open market. Estates often wait on probate before anyone can list. Owners behind on tax may face a May lien and need a closing date that clears it.

Some owners choose a cash sale for the certain closing date. The buyer accepts the house as-is, you skip the repair list, and open tax is taken from the proceeds. Weigh that against what fixing the house and carrying it through another bill would cost.

Beaches, water and what buyers ask

The town runs four Sound beaches: Greenwich Point, Byram Beach, Island Beach and Great Captain Island, all opened to non-residents after the 2001 Leydon v. Greenwich ruling. For a seller the shoreline comes down to flood zone mapping, drainage and the age of docks or seawalls. Waterfront buyers usually want insurance history before they offer, so collect it before you list. A short folder with flood certificates, past claims and repair receipts for any seawall or dock saves a week of back and forth later.

When are Greenwich property taxes due?

Payment is due July 1, and the bill turns delinquent a few weeks later. Check the Tax Collector's page each year, since mailing and delinquency dates can change.

Where do I file a Greenwich assessment appeal?

With the Board of Assessment Appeals, not the Assessor. The Board's email is boardofassessmentappeals@greenwichct.org.

Who sets the Greenwich mill rate?

The Board of Estimate and Taxation sets it in May. An assessment appeal does not change the rate.

What happens to Greenwich real estate that stays delinquent?

Interest builds up to a set date, and any property with a balance is liened in May. Call the Tax Collector for a payoff before you set a closing date, and ask whether a lien paper has already been recorded against the house.

Can I sell a Greenwich house if I owe back taxes?

Yes. Unpaid tax comes out of the proceeds at closing, and a cash sale can close on a date you choose.

Bridgeport became a town in 1821 and a city in 1836. Of its 19.4 square miles, 16.0 are land. The city stands only 3.3 feet above sea level, which explains why buyers ask about flooding and storms. Bridgeport grew up as a port and factory town, so housing age and condition swing widely between neighborhoods.

How the tax is calculated

Multiply the property's assessed value by the mill rate and you have the bill. A mill is $1 of tax on every $1,000 of assessment. The city's rates for fiscal year 2026-2027 are 27.95 mills for real estate and personal property and 31.75 mills for motor vehicles.

Due dates and delinquency

Assessment happens as of October 1. The tax is levied the following July 1 and collected in two installments. State law treats an installment as delinquent once the first day of the next month arrives without payment.

Interest and how payments are applied

Section 12-146 of the Connecticut General Statutes puts interest on the overdue part of a tax at 18 percent a year, counted from the original due date. A partial month counts as a full one. There is a $2 minimum per installment unless the municipality voted against it, and interest continues even after a judgment for the city.

Partial payments go first to interest and then to principal. Timeliness is judged by the municipal electronic payment service's timestamp or by the postmark on the envelope.

Take an assessment dispute to the Board of Assessment Appeals, in writing, by February 20 at the latest. The statute allows paper or email, in whatever way the board prescribes, and the Tax Assessor's office can hand you the current year's form. Your filing has to carry these items:

Each filer hears about the hearing's date, time and place by March 1, with at least seven calendar days of warning. A commercial, industrial, utility or apartment property assessed above $1 million may be denied a hearing, in which case the owner can head straight to Superior Court under section 12-117a.

A bill in arrears does not rule out a cash sale. The buyer takes the house as is, the title company requests the payoff figure, and what is owed comes out of the proceeds at closing. Three questions will come from the title company. Which installments are still open? Is a lien on file? Does anyone besides the owner of record have a right to sign? Settle them early. Each month a closing slips adds interest to a delinquent bill, so a clean file saves real money.

One more habit pays off: keep the paper trail. Save every notice, every receipt and any email from the collector. If the amount a closing agent quotes differs from your records, the file lets you ask a specific question and get a specific answer, and that is much faster than arguing from memory.

What should a seller do before listing?

Think in terms of the tax calendar. If it is spring and you believe the assessment is off, the filing window closes on February 20, so appeal before you sign a listing agreement. If a July or January installment is open, pay it or ask the collector for the exact amount including interest, so the buyer's attorney sees a clean record.

Next, ask the Tax Collector whether a lien was filed on the last June 30, and ask the Tax Assessor's office for the current year's application form if you plan to appeal. Finally, check your flood status and collect insurance papers. A seller who arrives with these items already settled usually negotiates from a stronger position, and a closing agent can finish the tax line without delay.

July 1 and January 1. An installment turns delinquent if it goes unpaid past the first day of the following month.

February 20 for the written appeal to the Board of Assessment Appeals, or March 20 if the assessor received an extension.

The 2022 revaluation and the phase-in choice

Waterbury finished a state-mandated five-year revaluation for the October 1, 2022 Grand List, and the new values went into use for the budget year that began July 1, 2023. Residential values rose much faster than commercial ones, so many homeowners saw higher bills even though the mill rate fell.

The Assessor's Office appraises property at market value as of the last revaluation date and assesses it at the state-mandated 70 percent ratio. It also processes exemption applications and answers questions about how a given assessment was set.

Norwalk in brief

Norwalk's six taxing districts

The city is divided into six taxing districts, and every district sets its own rate to match the services it delivers. That is why two houses a mile apart can see different bills. Learn your district before you quote a tax figure to a buyer.

The First, Second, Third and Sixth districts have their own elected officers, annual meetings and budgets. The Fourth and Fifth districts are not separate governments and make up the city proper. Some districts also run utilities:

  • The First Taxing District provides water to the Third, Fourth and Fifth districts.
  • The Second Taxing District reaches into South Norwalk, East Norwalk, West Norwalk, Rowayton and Silvermine, and it runs South Norwalk Electric and Water.

Ask the Tax Collector if your bill carries a district charge. If it does, expect a separate line for it on the payoff letter.

Neighborhoods, rail and the shoreline

Dozens of named neighborhoods make up the city, from Rowayton and Silvermine to South Norwalk, Cranbury and Oak Hills. Shoreline exposure, train access and lot size set them apart, and buyers shop on those traits.

  • Rowayton, East Norwalk and South Norwalk each have a Metro-North station.
  • The Danbury Branch stops at Merritt 7, and Interstate 95, the Merritt Parkway and Route 7 all run through the city. Norwalk Transit District buses meet at a transportation hub.

If you overpaid Norwalk property tax

State law sets a limited window for claiming back overpaid property tax. Under Section 12-129, a written application to the collector must be delivered or postmarked by the latest of three years from the tax due date, any longer deadline the municipality sets by ordinance, or 90 days after a final court order or statutory process deletes an item of assessment.

The municipality can deny a refund when the same owner has another tax delinquency, and it applies the overpayment to that debt instead. A short call goes faster when you have the basics in front of you. Have your street address and parcel details ready, and know whether you think you are in the First, Second, Third, Fourth, Fifth or Sixth district. If you are not sure, say so. The Tax Collector or the city's tax district map settles it.

Ask for the payoff in writing, with a good-through date that covers your expected closing. Then ask the Town Clerk's Land Records desk whether anything else is recorded against the property, such as an old mortgage that was never released. Sorting out a missing release before an offer is far easier than discovering it at the table.

Utility accounts come up at closing too. A house served by one of the taxing district utilities, or by Eversource, needs a final reading and a closed account in your name, so write down which provider you use.

Selling with taxes owed

Unpaid property tax does not block a Norwalk sale, because it can be paid off out of the proceeds. The sequence still matters. A typical run looks like this.

  2. Check the land records at the Town Clerk for any recorded lien or unreleased mortgage.

Danbury is organized into named districts instead of one grid, among them Mill Plain, Great Plain, Long Ridge, Germantown, Beaverbrook and Wooster Heights. A house on Long Ridge Road and another near downtown are worlds apart in a buyer's eyes, and an appraiser will price them accordingly. Known as the Hat City for its old hat industry, Danbury now draws buyers who commute on Interstate 84 or on the Metro-North Danbury Branch, which ends here.

How Danbury property tax is billed

The real estate bill arrives in July. The city's real estate FAQ lets a bill over $100 be paid in four pieces, due in July, October, January and April, while smaller ones are paid whole. The July piece covers July, August and September.

The assessment date is October 1 of the previous year. The FAQ illustrates it with a buyer who closed in January 2010 and still owed the bill built on the October 2009 list: assessed in arrears, paid current. Call the Tax Collector for the installment rules that apply now. A deed filed with the Town Clerk prompts the Assessor to change the owner's name and address on the parcel.

Who does what at City Hall

  • Assessor: values, appeals and changes of address.
  • Tax Collector: bills, payments and the payoff figure.

Three themes recur among Danbury sellers: aging systems, tenants in multi-unit houses and tax bills paid in installments.

  • An inherited house can have several unpaid installments, and because the list date is October 1, the first bill after a sale may carry the previous owner's name.
  • Landlords near downtown or the university may be selling with a lease already running.

The last one set values for the October 1, 2022 Grand List, with new bills due from July 2023. Connecticut requires a revaluation every five years.

New Britain housing in brief

New Britain is a Hartford County city about 9 miles southwest of Hartford, home to 74,135 people in 2020 within roughly 13.4 square miles. Stanley Black & Decker still has its headquarters here, a reminder of the Hardware City days when factories made locks and tools.

The housing stock is older and heavily rented. The 2020 census found 29,054 households and 31,510 housing units, with 7.8 percent of the units vacant. Who bills and who assesses

Two offices handle your tax. The Assessor sets the assessment, and the Tax Collector bills and collects. The Tax Collector's pages cover online payments, and the city's site is newbritainct.gov. Call the office or read your bill for exact installment dates and interest. The legal framework comes from Connecticut law, not the city. Chapter 204 of the General Statutes covers how taxes are levied and collected.

State options if you cannot pay

Connecticut gives cities a few tools for owners who are struggling. Section 12-124 lets a city's mayor and aldermen abate taxes, or the interest on delinquent taxes, for persons who are poor and unable to pay. The abatement needs the approval of a standing abatement committee or the state's Secretary of the Office of Policy and Management.

Section 12-124a lets a municipality abate tax that exceeds 8 percent of an owner-occupant's income, but only if the owner signs a reimbursement agreement. That agreement is recorded as a lien and comes due in full when the property is sold. Ask the Tax Collector whether New Britain offers it.

Chapter 204 also covers collection by suit, receivership of rents for delinquent taxes, and taxes that become uncollectible after fifteen years. If you are far behind, talk to a lawyer before assuming any of those apply to you.

Can you sell a New Britain house with taxes owed?

Yes. A sale closes after the title company confirms what is owed and pays it from the proceeds. The order that works best is simple.

  2. Ask your attorney to check for liens, including any recorded abatement lien.

A cash purchase suits owners whose house needs work, has tenants or sits in probate. Read any offer closely and compare it with the alternatives.

Working out a payoff step by step

Treat the payoff as a small project with a clear order. Begin with the bill: find the account number and the address exactly as the city lists them. Call the Tax Collector, give those details and ask what is owed, which installments are open and how interest is being added. Request the answer in writing, and ask the office to tell you if the number changes before your closing date.

Next, share the figure with your closing attorney or title company. They will run their own title search and look for liens, so ask them to tell you right away if anything turns up that you did not expect. The goal is to arrive at the closing table with no surprises, so that the tax is paid from the proceeds and the deed passes cleanly.

Finally, keep a record. A short note of each call, with the date, the person you spoke to and the amount quoted, is enough. It protects you if a figure is later questioned.

Asking for hardship relief before you sell

Abatement is not automatic, and a city may or may not offer each option, so treat it as a question to ask. Start with the Tax Collector and describe your situation plainly. If the office points you to an abatement process, find out who decides, what paperwork is required and how long a decision usually takes, because that timeline may affect when you can close. If you are told a reimbursement agreement is available, read it with your attorney first. A recorded lien under Section 12-124a becomes due in full when the property is sold, so it is paid out of your proceeds at closing and reduces what you take home.

For some owners, abatement is the right route because they plan to stay. For owners who have already decided to sell, a clean payoff and an as-is sale may be the shorter path. Weigh both with a lawyer before you commit to either.

What a cash sale skips

A sale to an as-is buyer leaves out several steps that a regular listing requires. You do not stage the house or host showings, you do not have to wait on a buyer's mortgage approval, and you do not pay for repairs a lender might demand. The title company still confirms the tax balance and pays it, along with any other recorded charge, from the proceeds. What you give up is the chance to wait for the highest possible price. For a house with deferred repairs, tenants or a probate delay, many owners decide the certainty is worth it. Whatever you choose, have your attorney read the contract before you sign.

Tenants, repairs and probate

Older wiring and plumbing are common in houses built around 1956, and buyers who use a mortgage may ask for repairs. A tenant-occupied house may need written notice before showings. A probate sale can take longer than a standard sale. Ask your attorney how each issue applies to your house, and ask the Assessor whether a recent permit or addition changed the assessed value.

For an inherited house, find out who has authority to sign before anything else. The estate must name a representative, and that person can request the payoff and sign the deed. For a house with tenants, read the lease and decide with your attorney how showings, access and any move-out date will be handled. A cash buyer who accepts the house as-is, tenants and repairs included, can shorten this list, but you should still compare the offer with a regular listing before deciding.

The city's Tax Collector bills and collects it, and the Assessor sets the assessment. Use the city's online payments page or call the office for balances.

Connecticut Section 12-124 lets a city abate taxes or interest for poor persons who are unable to pay, subject to approval. Ask the Tax Collector what New Britain offers.

What happens to an abatement lien when I sell?

Under Section 12-124a, a recorded reimbursement lien becomes due in full upon sale or transfer of the property, if the city adopted that option.

CTfastrak buses run from downtown to Hartford's Union Station, and the nearest Amtrak and Hartford Line station is in Berlin.

Yes. Back taxes are paid from the proceeds at closing, so ask for a written payoff before you accept an offer. Have your attorney read the contract too.

Shoreline houses

Fairfield has about 5 miles of Long Island Sound coastline, five lifeguarded town beaches and a good number of tidal creeks, so plenty of houses sit near water. Rivers and brooks cross town too, among them the Mill, the Rooster, Ash Creek and Sasco Brook, and newer homes keep going up in the Fairfield Beach area close to the sand.

Due dates and penalties

Real estate tax comes in four payments a year. A bill totaling $100 or less is collected in one piece with the first installment. The Tax Collector's warning is blunt: never set a bill aside. Disputes over value go to the Board of Assessment Appeals. On the 2026 Grand List the petition must be received at the Assessor's Office by 4:30 pm on Friday, February 19, 2027. A postmark earns you nothing. The town's appeals page has the form.

Email to assessor@fairfieldct.org is accepted. Each property needs its own petition, real estate filings should include the property card, and anyone speaking for you needs a notarized affidavit.

Two situations stretch a Fairfield timeline more than any repair. An estate has to name someone with authority to sign the deed, and the quarterly bills keep coming in the meantime. A rented house works differently: the tenant's lease usually runs past your preferred closing, so find out early whether the tenant plans to stay or leave, and put the answer in writing before you accept an offer.

What Fairfield sellers usually face

Aging houses on small lots, shoreline worries and a four-part tax calendar are the usual story. A house near the beach can carry deferred maintenance, so many owners order an inspection before they list. An inherited house may sit through several due dates while the estate settles who owns it. If tenants live there, the lease has to be dealt with before closing.

A cash sale skips most of that. The buyer takes the house as it stands, you do not schedule showings or fund repairs, and the title company settles any open tax from the proceeds. Weigh that against what repairs, showings and one more installment would cost you.

Getting ready for the Assessor's Office

If you plan to appeal before selling, a lower assessment can help the next owner and your own final bills. Pull your property card first and read it line by line. Wrong square footage, an extra bathroom or a finished basement that was never finished are the common errors. Bring photos and any recent sale prices for similar houses on your street.

Each hearing is 15 minutes, with sworn and recorded testimony. The Board decides later at a separate meeting and can raise or lower the assessment.

Hamden in brief

Hamden lies directly north of New Haven, with Cheshire and Wallingford above it, North Haven to the east and Woodbridge and Bethany to the west. The 2020 count was 61,169 residents across 33.4 square miles, and the ZIP codes are 06514, 06517 and 06518. Locals call it the Land of the Sleeping Giant, after the ridge in the north.

The town grew as a string of villages that still feel separate: Whitneyville, Spring Glen, Mount Carmel, Centerville, Highwood, Dunbar Hill, West Woods and others. The southern end runs into New Haven, and the north is more rural. Buyers compare villages before they compare houses, so know which one your listing will be filed under. Wilbur Cross Parkway and Route 40 give quick highway access, and Connecticut Transit buses run along Dixwell and Whitney Avenues.

The town's news page posts any change to the schedule, which has happened when the budget was adopted late. If a summer bill looks delayed, check there and call before assuming a due date.

How to appeal your Hamden assessment

Start with a written application filed with the Assessor's Office. The Board of Assessment Appeals then hears the case in March. The town's appeal procedure page showed an application window from February 2 through February 20 for the 2025 Grand List, so plan on a short February window each year and ask the Assessor for the next one.

Consideration of $2,000 or more triggers the tax unless an exemption fits. Have the deed, a government ID and any estate papers ready. An estate needs a clear deed and a person with authority to sign before a sale can record, and rental owners should be ready to show how the tenants will be handled before closing.

Sellers in Hamden come from many different village pockets, and the problems vary with the pocket. Rental owners often have to settle tenants before closing. Estates wait on probate. Older houses near the New Haven line may need roof or systems work that a mortgage-backed buyer will ask about.

Hamden splits the work. The Assessor sets the value of the property and takes appeals, and the Tax Office sends the bill and collects it. Mixing them up wastes time: the Tax Office cannot change an assessment, and the Assessor cannot tell you what you owe. Both sit in the Government Center at 2750 Dixwell Avenue, the Assessor on the lower level and the Tax Office on the main floor, so one trip can cover both if you plan it.

Bring the bill or account number, a photo ID, and your deed or closing paperwork if the house is changing hands. If you are acting for an estate, add the papers that name you as the person in charge. Staff can then give you a figure you can hand straight to a closing attorney.

From payoff to closing day

A sale with tax owed usually moves in a predictable line. You ask the Tax Office for a balance, the closing attorney or title company requests its own payoff in writing, the buyer signs, and the open amount is paid from your proceeds before the deed goes on the land records. The town clerk then records the deed together with the conveyance return. Nothing here requires you to bring cash to the table.

What slows things is not the tax itself but the surprises around it: a lien nobody mentioned, a tenant who has not agreed to leave, or an estate waiting on a signature. Raise each of those with your attorney on the first call rather than the last.

Preparing for a hearing

A 10-minute hearing leaves little room to wander, so decide your single strongest argument beforehand. Bring a few recent sales of comparable houses, photos of anything that hurts value, and a copy of the property record with errors marked. Interstate 95 and U.S. Route 1 cross the south of the city, the Wilbur Cross Parkway crosses the north, and the Metro-North New Haven Line stops at Milford station. Tax areas inside Milford

Milford has a mayor and a 15-member Board of Aldermen, three from each of five districts. The Aldermen adopt the budget that sets the mill rate, and the mayor has no veto over what they pass. Hartford housing in brief

Hartford is Connecticut's capital, a river city in Hartford County counted 121,054 residents in 2020, all inside roughly 18 square miles. Vacant land is scarce. Lots are small, plenty of buildings hold two or three units, and buyers weigh one street against the next rather than treating the city as a single market.

Flooding is part of the riverside history. In April 1909 the river reached 24.5 feet above low water and swamped part of the city, and it overflowed again in 1930. Expect basement and drainage questions if the house stands near the river. Humid summers and snowy winters wear down roofs, gutters and furnaces as well, and an older house with a tired roof or a damp cellar is nothing unusual. They still sell. A buyer taking the house as-is prices in the repairs instead of asking you to do them.

Real estate tax due dates

Real estate tax is paid in halves, one due July 1 and one due January 1. Each half has a final payment date, and if that date is a Saturday or Sunday the deadline becomes the next Monday. The schedule appears on the Tax Collector's Tax Information page.

Pay after that final date and interest accrues at 1.5% per month, which the city also quotes as 18% per year. Elderly owners whose applications are approved pay on a separate four-installment calendar: July 1, October 1, January 1 and April 1. It does not apply unless the city has approved your application.

Vehicle, personal property and abatement bills

Personal property and car tax run on the same July and January rhythm, with any bill above $100 divided into two payments. A car registered after October 2 receives a single supplemental bill due January 1.

Hardship relief goes through an abatement petition filed with the Tax Collector. It must be filled in completely, signed and notarized. The abatement committee gathers quarterly, and the city returns incomplete petitions without putting them on an agenda, so a missed signature or stamp can cost you a whole quarter before anyone looks at the case.

  • If you are about to register a vehicle, pay early. The DMV will not process the registration until the payment clears.
  • Cash, an in-person card or certified funds clear in about one business day, an online card in two, a check in ten.
  • Hold on to every receipt, because lost-receipt questions are on the office's own FAQ.

The Hartford closing: tax, deed and state form

On closing day the attorney or title company takes any unpaid property tax out of what you receive, and the deed is then recorded in Hartford. Since the tax year has two installments, a mid-year sale normally leaves one of them partly open, and the amount owed appears as its own line on the settlement statement.

The state wants its own paper filed with the deed. That is Form OP-236, the conveyance tax return, which the grantor, the grantor's attorney or an authorized agent hands to the town clerk at recording. It covers transfers of $2,000 or more unless an exemption applies, and the code for Hartford is 064. Instructions sit on the Department of Revenue Services conveyance tax page.

Two exemptions are worth a look if money is tight. A principal residence given up in lieu of foreclosure qualifies. So does one sold for less than the mortgages plus the real estate taxes and other lienable charges that outrank them. Your closing attorney can tell you whether either describes your sale.

Questions for the Hartford tax office

An online account summary can trail a payment you made yesterday, and only the office can state the true balance on an account. When you call, work from this list:

  • Which installments show as paid, and when is the next one due?
  • Has a lien been recorded, and what must happen for a release?
  • Is the bill still going to a mortgage company, or does it come to you?

Request the answers in writing. With a written payoff in hand, the title company can fix a firm number for closing, and you will know what is left for you after the tax is cleared.

How the payoff request works

Here is the quickest route. First, gather your account number from the latest bill, along with the parcel address as the city lists it. Third, pass the figure to your title company and ask them to confirm it against their own search. If your closing slips by a few weeks, the number can change, so ask for an updated figure rather than assuming the first one still holds.

Jot down who you spoke with, the date and the amount quoted, and keep the figure with your closing papers. If you rent the house out, tell the tenants why a title company may contact them, so a request for access or information does not come as a surprise.

You can. The unpaid tax is normally taken from your proceeds at closing, so it does not have to be paid up front. In order: request the payoff, check for a lien, give the numbers to the title company, and choose a closing date once those answers are in hand.

Many Hartford sellers hold inherited houses, vacant houses or multi-family buildings with tenants in place, and each of those adds a step. An estate needs someone authorized to sign. An occupied building needs a plan for access before anyone can see it. Because buyers here often care more about what condition the building is in than which street it is on, a house needing work can be easier to sell as-is than to repair and list.

Selling for cash also trims the timeline, since there is no lender appraisal or loan approval to wait on. Cash Home Buyers purchases Hartford houses as-is, including those with back taxes, and the title company settles what is owed from the proceeds.

When are Hartford property taxes due?

Real estate tax is due July 1 and January 1. The last days to pay are August 1 and February 1, moved to Monday when they fall on a weekend.

What interest does Hartford charge on late real estate tax?

Late balances accrue interest at 1.5% per month, which the city states as 18% per year. The charge starts once the last day to pay has gone by, so a short delay costs less than a long one.

Is there a different payment plan for elderly Hartford owners?

Yes, for approved applications only. It uses four installments, due July 1, October 1, January 1 and April 1.

Can I sell my Hartford house if I owe back taxes?

Yes, and many owners do. Closing normally pays the tax out of your proceeds, so you need not pay it first. Ask the tax office for the payoff and have your title company confirm the figure.

Who files the Connecticut conveyance tax return?

The grantor, the grantor's attorney or an authorized agent files Form OP-236 when the deed is recorded. Your closing attorney normally handles it for you.

Billing and due dates

Appraisers studied property sales in the 24 months before October 1, 2025 to see where values rose or fell, then applied those results to homes that had not sold. Liens, demand letters and unpaid bills

  • Building permits are not issued for a property with such a debt, and Neighborhood Preservation Program funding is held back.
  • Unpaid water and sewer bills can lead to shutoff or a recommendation for foreclosure.

  2. Ask separately about water and sewer, which are billed on their own cycle.

If the data collector visited, you may have been asked to confirm details by mail. Keep that mailer with your sale papers. If an adult was home for an inspection, it is worth recalling what was measured, since a corrected record helps the buyer as well as you.

Many Meriden houses are old enough that condition is the main hurdle. Owners often face a repair list, a lien or an estate that needs time. The city mails one bill each July. Real estate can be paid in four equal installments in July, October, January and April.

Manchester is revaluing every property for an October 1, 2026 assessment date. State law puts towns on a five-year cycle, and the Assessment Office's revaluation overview walks through each step. The town hired Tyler Technologies to do the work.

A new value is not a new bill by itself. The assessment is only one half of the tax calculation, and the rest depends on the mill rate the town sets. Older houses are the common thread. A house with outdated systems, a tenant in place or taxes behind can be hard to list on the open market. Some owners are also trying to decide whether to sell before or after the revaluation notices land, and that is worth a call to the Assessment Office.

Mill rates and how the tax is figured

Frequently asked questions

When are Middletown real estate taxes due?

July 1 and January 1. Interest at 1.5% per month starts if an installment is still unpaid on the first business day of the next month.

How does Middletown assess property?

Property is assessed at 70% of its value, and that assessment is multiplied by the mill rate.

What is the Middletown mill rate?

On the October 1, 2025 grand list the combined real estate rate is 40.800 mills in the City Fire District, 38.611 in the South Fire District and 35.384 in the Westfield Fire District.

Do some Middletown owners get two tax bills?

Yes. Those two districts bill and collect on their own, apart from the city bill.

Can I sell my Middletown house if I owe tax?

Yes. Closing normally settles the tax out of what you receive, with the title company making the payment.
